evidence_quotes.quote: In Dhaka, Bangladesh, sewer misconnections persist despite sewer infrastructure expansion by the Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (DWASA). This mixed-method cross-sectional study aimed to develop targeted, evidence-based interventions to increase sewer connections in urban communities. We surveyed 384 households and conducted 10 in-depth interviews and two focus group discussions across five DWASA zones.

Qualitative findings revealed widespread dissatisfaction with dysfunctional drainage systems, high connection costs, inadequate maintenance support from DWASA, and bureaucratic delays as significant barriers. These results highlight a complex interplay of psychological, financial, and administrative challenges limiting sewer uptake.

We wrote to them (DWASA). We gave them applications requesting maintenance. We went to their offices for support. However, they just told us it was not solely their responsibility (indicating the involvement of the city corporation).

DWASA bill is already burdening us, but we are not getting any service. I am connected to city corporation’s drain. And the cost of connecting new households to the sewer is also higher than connecting to city corporation drain. That fee should be reduced also
Respondents were split equally into connected to sewer (n = 192) and not-connected to sewer (n = 192).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household sanitation service access in urban Dhaka, Bangladesh, specifically household connection versus non-connection (and misconnection to storm/city corporation drains) to the official Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (DWASA) piped sewer network.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 (legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor), the paper clearly passes (plain=yes) because it investigates bureaucratic delays, administrative procedures, DWASA-city corporation institutional fragmentation, legal issues, and sewer tariffs/connection fees. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, the paper is borderline because its primary analytical framework applies the psychological RANAS model to design Behaviour Change Techniques (which alone would be excluded as behavioural promotion). However, it still passes the narrow reading (narrow=yes) because its primary empirical data directly measure and analyse rule-type mechanisms governing sewer access: (1) administrative burden and inter-agency regulatory structure (complicated DWASA connection application procedures, written applications and office visits deflected due to split DWASA vs. city corporation responsibility in Sections 3.3 and 3.7, survey item on 'No approval from city corporation' in Table 2, and procedural how-to knowledge in Table 3); (2) tariff and cost-recovery rules (mandatory monthly DWASA sewer bills charged even to unconnected properties in sewer-billed zones in Table 1 [median $27 vs. $22, p=0.0002] and Sections 3.3/3.8, plus high formal DWASA connection fees relative to city corporation drain connections); and (3) 'Legal issues' obstructing sewer connection tested across connected vs. non-connected households in Table 3 (mean difference -0.02, p=0.574, d=-0.06; non-significance never decides eligibility per the 2026-10-14 rule).
criterion_notes.c3: Primary cross-sectional mixed-methods empirical study conducted between October 2023 and November 2024, combining a stratified matched survey of 384 household owners (192 connected, 192 not-connected) with 10 in-depth interviews and 2 focus group discussions with unconnected landlords (note: shares the 384-household survey dataset with Alam et al., 2025, which should be checked for study-cluster deduplication during extraction).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household sewer connection status (connected to DWASA sewer n=192 vs. not-connected/misconnected to open or city corporation drainage n=192), satisfaction with current wastewater management access (55% vs. 30%, p<0.001), and anticipated barriers to future sewer connection.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (household owners/landlords in 10 neighbourhoods across 5 DWASA MODS zones in Dhaka; N=384 households in survey plus 10 IDIs and 2 FGDs), exposures (administrative burden/connection procedures, DWASA-city corporation jurisdictional split and approval, legal issues, DWASA sewer billing and connection-fee rules, alongside RANAS factors), outcomes (household DWASA sewer connection vs. non-connection), and study design (cross-sectional mixed-methods) are all clearly identified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods study (stratified matched household survey of 384 household owners plus 10 in-depth interviews and 2 focus group discussions)
population_and_sample: Urban household owners/landlords across 10 neighbourhoods in 5 DWASA Maintenance, Operation, Distribution, and Services (MODS) zones in Dhaka, Bangladesh: N = 384 surveyed household owners (192 connected to DWASA sewer and 192 not-connected to sewer), plus 10 male unconnected landlords in in-depth interviews and 2 focus group discussions (6-10 male participants each)
exposure: Administrative connection procedures and bureaucratic delays at DWASA, inter-agency jurisdictional division and municipal approval between DWASA and city corporations, legal issues, and DWASA tariff/monthly sewer billing and new-connection fee rules (examined alongside RANAS psychological factors)
outcome: Household connection to the official DWASA foul-water sewer network versus non-connection/misconnection to open or city corporation drains, satisfaction with current wastewater access, and perceived barriers to future sewer connection
rationale: Included under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (medium confidence). Although the study uses the psychological RANAS framework to propose Behaviour Change Techniques, it is an observational cross-sectional mixed-methods study (N = 384 households: 192 connected vs. 192 not-connected; 10 IDIs; 2 FGDs) whose primary quantitative and qualitative results directly examine rule-type mechanisms governing household sewer connection: administrative burden in DWASA connection procedures and written applications deflected due to DWASA-city corporation jurisdictional division, city corporation approval (Table 2), legal issues obstructing connection (Table 3; non-significant quantitative differences do not affect eligibility per the 2026-10-14 rule), and tariff/cost-recovery rules including high formal DWASA connection fees and mandatory monthly DWASA sewer billing imposed even on unconnected households discharging to city corporation drains (Table 1 and Sections 3.3 and 3.8). Note for extraction: the 384-household dataset overlaps with Alam et al. (2025) and should be checked for study-level clustering if Alam et al. (2025) is also in the corpus.
